rules.title: Ban on landlord application fees and other up-front charges
rules.requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a Massachusetts landlord (lessor) may require payment only of first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee. Application, pet, cleaning, amenity, and other fees are prohibited.
rules.key_value: Only first, last, security deposit, and lock fee may be collected; application fees prohibited
rules.coverage_conditions: All lessors of residential rental housing in Massachusetts, before the start of a tenancy.
rules.exemptions: Licensed real estate brokers may charge fees under 254 CMR 7.00. A landlord who is also a broker may likely charge only through a separate bona fide brokerage business, based on a non-binding Housing Court case.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Whether the fee is charged by a licensed broker rather than by the lessor.

rules.penalty: In Perry v. Equity Residential Management (D. Mass. 2014), the tenants were awarded treble damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees.
rules.quoted_span: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks ( MGL Ch 186 Section 15B ).
rules.conflict_note: The source says the law has been in effect since the 1970s but gives no exact effective date. Per the source, it is unsettled whether requiring an applicant to pay a third-party screening service violates the statute; attorneys' opinion is that requiring it is risky. Source is a secondary trade-association blog.

rules.title: Licensed brokers may charge prospective tenants fees with written disclosure
rules.requirement: Only licensed brokers or salespeople may charge prospective tenants a fee for finding housing. At the first personal meeting, the broker must give a signed written notice stating the fee amount, the time and manner of payment, and whether the fee depends on a lease being signed.
rules.coverage_conditions: Licensed real estate brokers and salespersons who find rental housing for prospective tenants for a fee.

coverage.unverifiable_conditions: Broker licensure status and whether the required written notice was given.

rules.quoted_span: Licensed brokers can charge fees to prospective tenants so long as the brokers comply with the board of registration’s regulations.
rules.conflict_note: Source is a secondary blog and gives no effective date. It is unsettled whether a landlord who is also a broker may charge a fee; Samia v. McElaney (Housing Court, 1983) is non-binding.
